C-sign grip over groin.text: Patients cup the hand in a 'C' shape over the anterior/lateral hip, thumb posterior over the trochanter and fingers gripping into the groin, to localize deep intra-articular pain. First described by Byrd, this gesture is a validated descriptor for FAI and labral pathology and helps differentiate deep joint pain from superficial lateral (trochanteric) or posterior (piriformis) pain generators.
C-sign grip over groin.source: Byrd, 2007 (C-sign); Reiman & Thorborg, hip clinical examination literature

antalgic gait.text: A shortened stance phase on the involved limb reduces the terminal-stance hip extension/internal-rotation moment, which would otherwise drive the femoral head into the anterosuperior acetabular rim — the impingement position. Avoiding this loading pattern is a protective gait adaptation in symptomatic FAI/labral tear.
antalgic gait.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment (hip gait); Reiman et al., hip impingement clinical presentation literature

Reduced hip IR posture.text: Patients rest the hip in relatively less internal rotation to keep the femoral head off the anterosuperior acetabular rim/labrum. Because flexion plus IR is the same combined position that provokes symptoms on the FADIR test, a guarded reduced-IR resting posture reflects the same underlying anterior impingement mechanism.
Reduced hip IR posture.source: Physio-pedia, FADIR test mechanics; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12 (Hip)

passive.label: Passive Flexion + overpressure with FADIR (adduction + IR at end-flexion)

findings: Resisted tests usually normal — not a contractile pattern
Passive FADIR (flexion + adduction + IR at end-flexion) with overpressure reproduces groin pain/click
sttt.interpretation: The passive FADIR provocation, not resisted testing, is what reproduces symptoms here — consistent with a labral/impingement source rather than a contractile lesion.

cpa.pattern: A Hip Extension Firing Order pattern for a QL/hamstring-dominant compensation. Fascial component (from source): Anterior hip capsule / adductor fascia.

kineticChain.name: Hip Internal Rotation Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: Moderately restricted (20–29°) internal rotation is explicitly documented as consistent with FAI, where the FADIR test is likely positive.

functionalScreen.name: Seated Hip Rotation (FAI + capsular screen)
functionalScreen.note: The named functional test for exactly this pattern. FMA source note: FADIR & deep squat reproduce groin pain/click.

H02.name: Hip Osteoarthritis
keyExams: Passive hip ROM with end-feel (capsular pattern)

Reduced stride.text: Shortened stride length reflects loss of terminal hip extension — typically the earliest range lost in hip OA as the anterior capsule and iliofemoral ligament contract — combined with pain-avoidant loading through late stance.
Reduced stride.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12 (capsular pattern of the hip)

gluteal/quad wasting.text: Disuse atrophy of the gluteals and quadriceps develops secondary to chronic pain-limited weight-bearing and reduced activity, a hallmark secondary sign in established hip OA distinguishing a chronic degenerative presentation from an acute mechanical one.

antalgic gait.text: A pain-avoidance gait pattern that shortens stance-phase duration on the arthritic hip, reducing joint reaction force, which reaches roughly three times body weight during single-leg stance.
antalgic gait.source: StatPearls, Trendelenburg Gait (hip joint loading during stance phase)

Fixed-flexion / externally-rotated postu.text: This resting posture reflects the classic OA capsular pattern — the hip settles into flexion and external rotation because the anterior capsule and iliofemoral ligament contract first, restricting extension and internal rotation before abduction (capsular pattern: IR = Flexion = Abduction restricted, extension lost earliest).
Fixed-flexion / externally-rotated postu.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12 (capsular pattern of the hip); Cyriax capsular pattern concept

findings: Passive IR most restricted — capsular pattern IR = Flexion = Abduction
sttt.interpretation: A capsular pattern (IR = Flexion = Abduction) with a hard/bony end-feel and painless resisted testing is consistent with osteoarthritic capsular restriction rather than a contractile lesion.

cpa.pattern: Check the Hip Extension Firing Order (often QL- or hamstring-dominant). Fascial component (from source): Global hip capsular fascial restriction.

kineticChain.name: Hip Internal Rotation Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: Severely restricted, often <20° with significant asymmetry — matching the capsular-pattern IR loss on passive testing above.

functionalScreen.name: Seated Hip Rotation

fields.label: Seated Hip Rotation
options: Bilateral, more severe restriction, hard/bony end-feel (OA)

functionalScreen.note: Same test as FAI, but expect bilateral, more severe restriction with a hard/bony end-feel. FMA source note: Capsular-pattern loss (IR/flexion); squat & stairs limited.

Tender over greater trochanter.text: Direct point tenderness over the trochanteric facets is the hallmark localizing sign of gluteal tendinopathy — the gluteus medius and minimus tendons insert here, and their compressive loading against the trochanter (especially in adduction) is the primary pain generator in GTPS.
Tender over greater trochanter.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12; Grimaldi, gluteal tendinopathy compressive-load literature

Trendelenburg.text: A positive Trendelenburg sign reflects gluteus medius/minimus weakness or pain-inhibition failing to stabilize the pelvis in single-leg stance, causing a contralateral pelvic drop — direct evidence of the abductor mechanism dysfunction underlying GTPS.

Hip-drop / adducted stance (compensating.text: Standing with the pelvis dropped and the hip adducted increases iliotibial band tension and compresses the gluteal tendons against the greater trochanter — patients often unconsciously shift out of this position, or adopt it as a compensatory stance reflecting glute medius weakness/inhibition.
Hip-drop / adducted stance (compensating.source: Grimaldi, gluteal tendinopathy compressive-load literature; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12

findings: Resisted abduction strong but painful at the trochanter
Passive adduction (Ober-type stretch) reproduces lateral pain
sttt.interpretation: Strong-but-painful resisted abduction localizing to the trochanter, plus a positive Ober-type passive stretch, is the classic contractile (tendon) pattern for gluteal tendinopathy.

cpa.pattern: The textbook GTPS driver — confirm via therapy localization (touch TFL, retest glute med). Fascial component (from source): Lateral line (ITB/TFL) tension.

kineticChain.name: Hip Abduction Mobility & Stability (Trendelenburg + Ober's)
kineticChain.chainEffect: Documents both the mobility restriction and the stability deficit — the direct match for lateral hip pathology.

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Squat + Lateral Step Down

fields.label: Single Leg Squat (glute med / dynamic valgus)

functionalScreen.note: Both are the app's named functional tests for this exact pattern. FMA source note: Single-leg stance 30s & resisted abduction reproduce lateral pain.

Ischial tuberosity tenderness.text: Tenderness directly over the ischial tuberosity localizes pathology to the common hamstring tendon origin (semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris), the classic site of proximal hamstring tendinopathy.
Ischial tuberosity tenderness.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12; Cyriax contractile-lesion localization principle

Posterior pelvic-tilt sitting avoidance.text: A posterior pelvic tilt increases hip flexion at the pelvis relative to the femur, which lengthens the hamstring origin and compresses it against the ischial tuberosity/seat surface — patients with proximal hamstring tendinopathy characteristically avoid this position (and prolonged sitting generally) because it reproduces their pain.
Posterior pelvic-tilt sitting avoidance.source: Musick et al., proximal hamstring tendinopathy load-management literature

Ischial tuberosity.text: Point tenderness at the tendon origin confirms the site of the tendinopathic/enthesis lesion, consistent with the Cyriax principle that a contractile lesion is localized by palpation combined with a painful resisted test (here, resisted hip extension) in that muscle's direction of action.
Ischial tuberosity.source: Cyriax, Textbook of Orthopaedic Medicine (contractile lesion pattern)

resisted.label: Resisted Hip Extension (knee extended, adding hamstring)

findings: Resisted hip extension (knee extended) strong but painful at the ischium — classic contractile pattern
Passive hip flexion with knee extended also reproduces pain
sttt.interpretation: Strong-but-painful resisted extension localizing to the ischium is the classic Cyriax contractile-lesion pattern for the proximal hamstring origin.

cpa.pattern: The classic driver: hamstrings become the primary hip extensor and get overloaded. Fascial component (from source): Posterior-chain (hamstring–sacrotuberous) fascia.

kineticChain.name: Hip Extension Mobility (Thomas Test)
kineticChain.chainEffect: Provides posterior-chain context, but the Prone Hip Extension functional test below is the more direct diagnostic tool for this condition.

functionalScreen.name: Prone Hip Extension (glute max firing pattern, Janda)
functionalScreen.note: Palpate glute max vs hamstring during the test — hamstring firing first/dominating is the direct functional correlate of this condition. FMA source note: Bent-knee stretch / long-lever resisted knee-flexion reproduce pain.

H05.name: Adductor-Related Groin Pain (Adductor Strain / Athletic Pubalgia)

Adductor-origin tenderness.text: Tenderness at the pubic adductor origin — most commonly adductor longus — is the hallmark localizing sign of adductor-related groin pain, reflecting tendinopathic or acute strain change at the tenoperiosteal junction.
Adductor-origin tenderness.source: Doha Agreement classification of groin pain in athletes; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12

± swelling.text: Localized swelling, when present, suggests a more acute musculotendinous strain with associated edema/hemorrhage rather than a purely chronic tendinopathic presentation, helping stage the injury (acute strain vs. chronic overuse).
± swelling.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12 (muscle strain grading)

Pelvic instability posture.text: An asymmetric or guarded pelvic posture reflects disrupted load transfer through the pubic symphysis and anterior pelvis — the adductors, rectus abdominis, and pelvic floor share a common aponeurosis at the symphysis, so instability here is characteristic of athletic pubalgia rather than an isolated peripheral muscle strain.
Pelvic instability posture.source: Doha Agreement classification of groin pain in athletes (pubic-related and adductor-related groin pain overlap)

Adductor origin.text: Point tenderness at the proximal adductor longus tenobony junction — the most common site of adductor-related groin pain — confirms the contractile source consistent with a positive resisted adduction/squeeze test.
Adductor origin.source: Doha Agreement classification of groin pain in athletes

Pubic ramus.text: Tenderness extending onto the pubic ramus suggests involvement of the symphyseal/parasymphyseal region (osteitis pubis or athletic pubalgia) rather than an isolated muscle-belly strain — an important differentiator that broadens the differential beyond a simple adductor strain.
Pubic ramus.source: Doha Agreement classification of groin pain in athletes

findings: Resisted adduction strong but painful at the pubic origin — the squeeze test is this same resisted test
Passive abduction (stretch) also reproduces groin pain
sttt.interpretation: Strong-but-painful resisted adduction localizing to the pubic origin, reproduced by the squeeze test, is the classic contractile pattern for adductor-related groin pain.

cpa.pattern: Typically compensating for an inhibited Glute Max — check the Hip Extension Firing Order. Fascial component (from source): Adductor / deep-front-line fascia.

kineticChain.reason: No hip KC test isolates pure adduction in this app's library (IR/ER/extension/abduction are covered, not adduction specifically) — rely on the resisted/CPA findings above.

functionalScreen.name: Hip Hinge Pattern or Single Leg Squat

fields.label: Single Leg Squat (compensatory pattern under loaded groin activity)

functionalScreen.note: Either test screens for compensatory patterns during loaded groin activity; choose per presentation. FMA source note: Resisted adduction (squeeze test) & change-of-direction reproduce pain.

Deep buttock tenderness.text: Tenderness localized deep in the buttock, over the piriformis muscle belly rather than the ischial tuberosity or trochanter, points to the deep gluteal space as the source — the key finding distinguishing this condition from proximal hamstring tendinopathy (H04) or GTPS (H03).
Deep buttock tenderness.source: Physiotutors, FAIR test / deep gluteal syndrome clinical reasoning

± sciatic signs.text: Radiating or neural-type symptoms occur because in a notable minority of people the sciatic nerve passes through or is closely related to the piriformis muscle; spasm, hypertrophy, or tightness of the muscle can irritate or compress the nerve, producing sciatica-like referral without a lumbar spine source (deep gluteal syndrome).
± sciatic signs.source: Physiotutors, FAIR test / piriformis-sciatic nerve anatomic relationship

Externally-rotated resting hip.text: The piriformis is a hip external rotator; a shortened/overactive piriformis can hold the resting hip in relative external rotation, and patients also tend to favor ER at rest because it slackens the piriformis and reduces tension on an irritated sciatic nerve.
Externally-rotated resting hip.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12; Physiotutors, FAIR test mechanics

passive.label: FAIR Test (passive hip flexion + adduction + IR)

findings: Resisted ER (piriformis) reproduces deep buttock pain
FAIR test (passive flexion + adduction + IR) is positive — the key provocation
sttt.interpretation: Resisted ER reproducing deep buttock pain, combined with a positive FAIR test, localizes the lesion to the piriformis/deep gluteal space.

muscles.name: Piriformis
muscles.state: Overactive, glute med compensation (or glute max)

cpa.pattern: Always check Glute Med/Glute Max facilitation before treating piriformis alone. Fascial component (from source): Deep gluteal fascial compartment; sciatic neural bias.

kineticChain.name: Hip External Rotation Mobility
kineticChain.chainEffect: Restricted external rotation with deep buttock pain is explicitly documented as consistent with piriformis syndrome, where the FAIR test is likely positive.

functionalScreen.name: Seated Hip Rotation (IR/ER range screen)
functionalScreen.note: Cross-reference against the FAIR-test finding above.

H07.name: Snapping Hip Syndrome (Coxa Saltans, Internal or External)
keyExams: Dynamic snapping hip test (observe/palpate active flexion-extension)

Visible/audible snap with movement.text: The defining sign of coxa saltans: in the internal type, the iliopsoas tendon catches and releases over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head as the hip moves from flexion to extension; in the external type, the iliotibial band/gluteus maximus snaps over the greater trochanter during flexion-extension. The snap itself, not pain, is the primary diagnostic feature in most cases (painless snapping is more common than painful).
Visible/audible snap with movement.source: StatPearls, Snapping Hip Syndrome (internal vs. external mechanism)

ITB-tight or hip-flexor-tight posture.text: A tight iliotibial band/TFL increases the band's tension and compressive contact against the greater trochanter (external type), while a tight iliopsoas increases its tension and contact against the iliopectineal eminence/femoral head (internal type) — either predisposes to the catching mechanism that produces the snap during hip flexion-extension.
ITB-tight or hip-flexor-tight posture.source: StatPearls, Snapping Hip Syndrome; Orthobullets, Coxa Saltans

findings: Resisted hip flexion (iliopsoas type) or resisted abduction (ITB type) may reproduce the snap
Mostly a dynamic/observational finding rather than a static resisted one
sttt.interpretation: These resisted tests are secondary here — the dynamic snapping hip test (active flexion-extension) is the primary provocation for this condition, per the source.

cpa.pattern: Check Glute Med facilitation in both types. Fascial component (from source): Lateral line (external) or iliopsoas (internal) fascia.

kineticChain.name: Hip Abduction Mobility (external/TFL type) or Hip Extension Mobility / Thomas Test (internal/iliopsoas type)

fields.label: Hip Extension Mobility / Thomas Test (internal/iliopsoas type)

kineticChain.chainEffect: Select per the suspected snapping structure — external (ITB) vs internal (iliopsoas).

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Squat or Hip Hinge Pattern

fields.label: Dynamic snap observed during loaded movement

functionalScreen.note: Observing the dynamic snap during a loaded functional movement is more revealing than any static positional test for this condition.
